title: Clinical Clerkships in Europe
paragraphs: From March this year, I was sent as an exchange student for one month to the University of Warwick in the UK and for two months to the University of Freiburg in Germany, and I was able to take part in clinical clerkships. It is often felt that the center of world medicine is now the United States, but I was able to catch a glimpse of healthcare in Europe, which has a different historical background from the competitive society of the US and a generous social security system. The University of Warwick, in Coventry in central England, had only just established its medical school in 2000. It has a four-year curriculum for graduates, and it sent out its first graduates last year. (A regular medical school has a five-year curriculum.) I was the first exchange student to do a clerkship there. Unlike the US, there is not much accurate information about healthcare in the UK, so I would like to include that perspective in my report. Students who graduate from a UK medical school rotate through the departments for one year as a Junior House Officer and for two to three years as a Senior House Officer (SHO), and then choose whether to become a specialist or a general practitioner (GP). After that, specialists train for several years as Registrars and obtain the position of Consultant, a senior doctor, which allows them to have their own patients. GPs, on the other hand, train at a clinic for several years and then become independent. I did clerkships in cardiology, A&E (acute and emergency), and GP. In the UK, each person is registered with a family doctor according to their address, and in order to see a specialist, they must receive a referral from the GP or go to the emergency department and be referred from there. In that sense, I did my clerkships in the reverse order of the route patients take when they seek care. In the first rotation, cardiology, one Registrar and one SHO were assigned under the consultant, and the three formed a team. There were five consultants, and each was on call for one week at a time and accepted all new patients. After that, the team follows them. Managing the ward is mainly the work of the SHO, the consultant concentrates on outpatients and cardiac catheterisation, and the Registrar learns techniques under the consultant. The consultant and the Registrar have a light burden of ward management, and secretaries do all the paperwork, so the consultant can concentrate on treatment and teaching, and the Registrar on improving technique. In A&E, where I went next, the SHOs were the main workforce. The SHO examined the patient and decided the treatment plan, consulted a senior doctor, and then consulted each department as needed. It was basically the same as emergency medicine in Japan, but doctors also work properly scheduled shifts, and I was told that working-hour limits are set so that SHOs in particular cannot work long hours. I was also allowed to examine patients in English, which I was not used to, but since I had no experience of prescribing, it was beyond my ability to take charge of a patient on my own. The GP rotation, which I did last, is probably the system most different from Japan. It is a so-called clinic without beds, in which several doctors share the outpatient work. GP practices, like hospitals, are run by the government agency NHS, but all tests such as blood tests are done at the hospital (there was not even an electrocardiograph), and GPs are mainly in charge of primary care and follow-up after specialist treatment. However, a system that connects all test data online with hospitals was recently introduced, and a system to screen for disease risk is also built in, and I was impressed that cooperation between hospitals and clinics is very advanced in terms of systems. About UK healthcare, I had heard rather bad rumours: long waiting times in emergency departments, waits of several months to see a specialist, difficulty getting an appointment with a GP quickly, growing patient dissatisfaction, and falling motivation among doctors because of a worsening working environment. But this was probably the situation until a few years ago, and my actual impression was different. In 2000 the Blair government announced policies to increase healthcare spending by 1.5 times and to increase the number of doctors, and these seem to be steadily producing results. In fact, although access feels somewhat worse than in Japan, the waiting time in emergency departments is no longer very different from Japan, and above all, medical care is basically free. Patient satisfaction also seems to have improved considerably, and doctors' working conditions also seem to be considerably better than in Japan. It seemed to me that the UK healthcare system, which takes a different direction from that of the US, has much to teach us as one way of providing healthcare.

Next, the University of Freiburg in Germany, where I did my clerkships after that, is a university with history and tradition in the small city of Freiburg in southwestern Germany. There I rotated through cardiovascular surgery, neurology and anesthesiology. German medical students complete lectures, examinations and clerkships in five years, and the sixth year is called PJ (Praktisches Jahr), in which, although they are still students, they are incorporated into the ward and take part in actual medical care as a member of the staff. In cardiovascular surgery, there was a conference from 7 a.m., after which the students did chores such as blood sampling and then did ward rounds with the doctor in charge of the ward. After that, we did administrative work such as examining new patients, examining patients before discharge and writing summaries, and the evening came in no time. If you cannot speak German, you of course cannot do the paperwork, and it is difficult to examine patients on your own, but I think there are many opportunities for procedures. About twice a week, I was able to scrub in and assist in the operating room. Basically two rooms were used every day, with two to three operations in each, and I was told there are 800 operations a year (and that this is still on the low side for cardiovascular surgery in Germany). So the senior doctors are truly immersed in surgery every day, and I thought it was an ideal environment for a surgeon. In neurology, where I rotated next, there were fewer patients, partly because of the strike by university hospital doctors that was being held across Germany at the time (!). I did my clerkship in the stroke unit. Since intensive care for the acute phase is provided here, it runs 24 hours a day, and the doctors also worked in eight-hour shifts. The students' main work was to examine patients who had stabilised and to make charts for handover. These charts were extremely detailed, and by the time I had updated them and performed the necessary procedures and tests, it was already time for handover. At first glance it seemed to be wasted work, but this is probably a necessary cost of operating a shift system. In anesthesiology, I was allowed to do various procedures such as intubation. In Germany, I was told that all anesthesia is handled by anesthesiologists, and anesthesia was completely led by anesthesiologists. Surgeon-administered anesthesia is reportedly unthinkable. Drugs not approved in Japan were also used, and the very smooth anesthesia left an impression on me. Once the anesthesia was stable, I could also receive various lectures. Healthcare in Germany has a universal insurance system.

Patients pay insurance premiums every month, and consultations and treatment are basically free. There is also a family doctor system, which seems to be the European style. The number of doctors per population is more than 1.5 times that of Japan, so staffing is very generous, but German doctors seem to have various complaints (although German doctors always take several weeks of vacation...), and there is reportedly a tendency for doctors to leave the country. This was also the cause of the strike, and I, who had never imagined a doctors' strike, was quite surprised. Patients must also suffer disadvantages because of it, but I did not get the impression that they were very dissatisfied, and it was also impressive that society seemed to regard doctors' assertion of their rights as a matter of course. I have ended up focusing on systems, but both the UK and Germany have numerous historic buildings and cultural facilities, and you can fully enjoy painting, music, football and so on, according to your tastes. In particular, this time my stay overlapped with the World Cup, so I cheered for Germany together with the students on the ward, watched Japan's match in the stadium, and even took part in a medical school football (or rather, casual) tournament held across Germany, and so I spent a very fulfilling time besides the clerkships. I would like to take this opportunity to thank again the professors and administrative staff of the International Exchange Office who gave me such a valuable opportunity, and I sincerely hope that as many people as possible will take up the challenge of clerkships abroad.
